analysis.one_liner: Creates a government-run Medicare drug plan that negotiates drug prices and strengthens low-income senior protections.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote: referred to two House committees when it was introduced in late September 2006, it sat in a health subcommittee until the Congress ended without any further action.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have let Medicare itself offer a prescription drug plan covering the whole country, with the government negotiating prices directly with drug manufacturers instead of leaving pricing to private insurers. It would also have rolled protections out for low-income seniors: wiping out copays for many people on both Medicare and Medicaid, fast-tracking subsidy applications using tax data, raising the asset limits to qualify, and blocking plans from dropping drugs from their lists mid-year. It would have cut payments to private Medicare Advantage insurers, including eliminating a fund created in the 2003 Medicare law, and it would have protected Social Security checks from being shrunk by rising drug-plan premiums.
analysis.who_benefits: Medicare beneficiaries, especially the roughly dual-eligible and low-income seniors who would get cost-sharing eliminated, faster subsidies, higher asset limits, and penalties waived; all seniors would gain access to a nationally uniform Medicare-run drug plan whose negotiated prices could be used to shrink the coverage gap. Community pharmacies would gain guaranteed dispensing fees and prompt-payment rules.

how_it_helps.text: The Secretary of Health and Human Services would have to offer one or more Medicare-operated drug plans covering the entire United States and negotiate directly with pharmaceutical manufacturers to reduce purchase prices, with savings usable to shrink the coverage gap [S2, S3].

The monthly premium for the Medicare-operated plan would be uniform nationwide, and subsidy-eligible individuals would be automatically enrolled in it, with notice and the right to choose another plan [S2, S3].

Cost-sharing would be eliminated for certain full-benefit dual eligibles (people on both Medicare and Medicaid), the indexing of price-sharing for low-income beneficiaries would end, and reimbursements would cover copays they paid in 2006 [S2, S3].

Low-income subsidies would be expedited using IRS tax-return screening, asset limits would rise to $50,000 per individual ($100,000 for couples), life insurance would no longer count as an asset, and the late-enrollment penalty would be waived for the first 24 months for subsidy-eligible people [S3].
Social Security benefits would be protected against decreases caused by Part D premium increases, with the government paying plans for the premium reductions [S2, S3].

Plans could not remove a covered drug from the formulary, worsen its tier, or add barriers like prior authorization without advance notice effective only the next January 1; formularies must cover all or substantially all drugs in six protected classes (including antidepressants, antipsychotics, and anticonvulsants), and the exclusion of benzodiazepines would be lifted [S2, S3].

The Medicare Advantage Regional Stabilization Fund would be eliminated and certain Medicare Advantage overpayments cut, and fraudulent enrollment would carry a 3-to-10-year criminal penalty, with a complaint process for people enrolled in plans without their consent [S2, S3].

Plans would have to pay clean claims within 14 days (electronic) or 30 days, with interest for late payment, and pay pharmacies a minimum dispensing fee on generics — the greater of 50% above the brand-name fee or $10 — to encourage generic use [S2, S3].

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name drug manufacturers would be paid less under government-negotiated prices; private Part D and Medicare Advantage insurers would face a government competitor, lose the stabilization fund and certain overpayments, and absorb new formulary, prompt-payment, and pharmacy-fee requirements; the federal government would bear the cost of eliminating cost-sharing, protecting Social Security checks from premium increases, and expanded low-income subsidies.
analysis.who_pays_short: Drug makers and private drug plans

drawbacks.text: The bill's generous new benefits are not paid for within its text: eliminating cost-sharing for dual eligibles, protecting Social Security checks from premium increases, and higher dispensing fees would all add federal spending, and the bill includes no offsetting revenue beyond the Medicare Advantage cuts and unknown savings from price negotiation [S3].

The subsidy screening would give the Health and Human Services Secretary access to taxpayers' IRS return information to identify likely-eligible seniors, a real privacy trade-off the bill attempts to limit with use restrictions and a one-year sunset on the disclosure authority [S3].
The formulary protections bar plans from removing drugs or adding restrictions like prior authorization mid-year even to manage costs, limiting the tools private plans use to hold down premiums [S3].

A single Medicare-operated plan with nationally uniform premiums could crowd out private drug plans; the bill acknowledges this competition by repealing the fallback plan provisions and auto-enrolling subsidy-eligible people into the government plan, while giving enrollees the right to switch [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits for seniors are direct and concrete: a national public plan with negotiated prices, zero copays for many of the poorest beneficiaries, and a guarantee that Social Security checks cannot be eaten up by rising premiums. The main costs fall on drug makers and private insurers through lower prices and lost subsidies, and on the federal Treasury through the low-income expansions, which the bill does not fully offset — an honest supporter would have to concede the fiscal hole. The design is workable rather than sloppy: it keeps private plans in place and lets beneficiaries opt out of the government plan, but the scale of the price-negotiation savings was never scored, so the affordability claim rests on untested estimates.

outcome.mechanism: Introduced with about three months left in the two-year session, it was sent to two House committees and then to a health subcommittee, and no hearing, markup, or vote ever followed before the Congress ended on January 3, 2007.

narrative.text: Rep. Lloyd Doggett (D-TX) introduced the bill on September 29, 2006, near the end of the 109th Congress [S1, S5].
Forty-three House Democrats cosponsored it; every sponsor and cosponsor was a Democrat [S4].
The same day, the House referred it to the Energy and Commerce Committee and the Ways and Means Committee [S5].
On October 2, 2006, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Health — the last action ever taken on the bill [S5].
Neither committee scheduled a hearing or markup, the bill never reached the House floor, and the Congress expired on January 3, 2007, killing the bill [S1, S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Private prescription drug plan sponsors and Medicare Advantage insurers are better off: no government-run competitor was created, subsidy-eligible beneficiaries were not auto-enrolled into it, and the Regional Stabilization Fund and certain Medicare Advantage overpayments survived. Brand-name drug makers also benefited, since government price negotiation never happened.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Private drug plans and drug makers

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.role: Committee of primary referral (chaired by Rep. Joe Barton, R-TX)
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup after the bill was referred to it on September 29, 2006

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: Second committee of referral (chaired by Rep. Bill Thomas, R-CA)
against.what_they_did: Never acted on the bill after referral, leaving it to die in the Subcommittee on Health

sides.party_line_note: All 44 sponsors and cosponsors were House Democrats; the bill died in committees controlled by the Republican majority without a hearing, markup, or vote, so the fight never produced a roll call.

industries.note: The bill would have required HHS to negotiate purchase prices directly with manufacturers and push cheaper therapeutic equivalents, cutting what drug companies are paid under Medicare Part D. Their interest in keeping the 2003 law's no-negotiation structure ran against seniors' interest in lower prices.

industries.industry: Private Medicare Part D prescription drug plans
industries.note: A Medicare-operated plan competing nationwide, auto-enrollment of subsidy-eligible beneficiaries into it, repeal of the fallback plan framework, and new formulary, prompt-payment, and pharmacy-fee rules would have shrunk the private plans' market and raised their costs. The bill locked in no new role for them; their gain from the bill's death was keeping the Part D market as designed in 2003.

The bill would have eliminated the Medicare Advantage Regional Stabilization Fund and extended the phase-out of certain Medicare Advantage overpayments beyond 2010, cutting federal payments to these insurers. Those payments came at the expense of taxpayers and, in the bill's framing, of fair pricing in the drug program.

The bill would have guaranteed pharmacies a minimum dispensing fee on generic drugs (at least the greater of 50% above the brand-name fee or $10), required prompt payment of clean claims within 14 to 30 days with interest, required plans to pay for medication therapy management based on time and intensity, and required plan networks to include enough retail pharmacies. These provisions improved pharmacists' revenue while keeping affordable drugs accessible to beneficiaries.
